of our municipal authorities, says the
Scientific American, to see that each city
is supplied with pure gas for illumination.
They should, therefore, not unfrequently
have the gas as it comes from the burn-
ing pipes, analyzed by competent chem-
ists. We are confident that much of the

companies is impure. All coals contain
carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen; and
bituminous coals in general contain
some sulphur. In the distillation of coal

quantity of ammonia comes over,
which, if not completely separated, is
carried off with the gas, and detracts
from its illuminating powers. It is also
injurious to the people by mixing with
the atmosphere, and being inhaled at
respiration. Being exceedingly vol-
atile, and yet not difficult to condense,
much of it escapes through leaks in the
gas conductors, and condenses in the soil
beneath the streets and buildings; this
is evident when any of our streets are
trenched for the purpose of examining
pipes or opening drains. An odor of
ammonia is always observable for a con-
siderable space around an exposed exca-
vation. If this is the case now, how
much worse must the evil be in nine or
ten years from the present date!

an impurity in the soil beneath our
streets, will, in the course of time, find

mosphere and pollute it. Nothing but

ments where gas is burned. Cannel

cannel in place of bituminous coal, they
